# On the strange comfort of small failures

I've been thinking about how we're taught to fear failure, but there's something oddly soothing about small, private ones.

Like when you mispronounce a word in your head for years, then learn the truth. Or when you're confidently wrong about something nobody asked you about. There's this moment of—deflation, sure—but also relief. The secret's out. You can stop maintaining it.

I think we accumulate these tiny fictions about ourselves without meaning to. How we thought photosynthesis worked. That we were bad at math (maybe you just had one bad teacher). That we're "not a morning person" (how many mornings did we actually try?). These aren't big enough to address directly, so they just... calcify.

Then something small punctures one and it's almost pleasant. Like lancing a blister you didn't know was bothering you.

The bigger failures—the ones that actually matter—those stay sharp and bad for a long time. But the small ones? They're kind of useful. They're like your brain's immune system, keeping you honest in the margins.

Maybe that's why people keep learning new things even when they're old. Not because they want to succeed, but because they've made peace with the fact that small failures feel better than the weight of never trying.

What small thing have you been wrong about for a while?
